about.title: About
about.heading: About Logia
about.dek: A free, open library of Christian commentary, set verse by verse beside Scripture.
what: Logia sets each verse of the Bible beside what the church has said about it, from the early church to the 1800s. It is free to read, free to share, and its data is open for anyone to build on, in the spirit of Sefaria's library of Jewish texts.
about.name_note: These are the words of Romans 3:2 for “the oracles of God”, which the Open Word Bible renders “the very words of God”. Logia takes its name from them, and from Papias's lost *Exposition of the Logia of the Lord*, one of the first Christian commentaries.
about.voices: Logia takes no side where Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings differ. Each commentator's words are kept whole, even where they are harsh or dated: a note may explain, but nothing is cut silently.
about.traditions: Traditions in the library so far
about.checked: Every excerpt is copied from a public-domain edition and never rewritten. These are the five steps each one goes through, shown for one real excerpt.
steps: A page scan on archive.org or a transcription on CCEL, published in 1930 or earlier.
The page Logia copies from is kept in the repository, with its address and when it was fetched.
A script finds each excerpt in its source: word for word, or in runs of six words for a scan.
Where a scan misread the printed page, the fix is a pair kept in the open data.
The excerpt appears on Logia beside the verse it comments on, linked to the full text.
about.trail_scan: Found in its source in runs of six words, as a page scan.
about.trail_digital: Found in its source word for word, as a transcription.
about.trail_fix: The scan read “{a}”; the page reads “{b}”.
about.steps_note: Every one of the {n} excerpts goes through these steps; {fixes} scan misreadings are corrected in all.
about.details_text: Every excerpt is copied from a public-domain edition, never rewritten, and the source text it came from is kept beside it. A script checks each excerpt against its source on every change: word for word for a transcription, and in runs of six words for a page scan, whose lines carry margin notes and running heads. Where a scan misread a letter (“Let ns” for “Let us”), the correction is listed openly and applied when the site is built.
bible: Logia reads the Open Word Bible, a CC0 translation from Hebrew and Greek with the reasoning behind every sentence. Logia never edits it: it is imported at a pinned version from the Open Word Bible's own repository.
languages: Logia starts in English. Each new language is translated from the best public-domain source, the original Greek, Latin or German where that is better than the English, and reviewed by native speakers before it is marked reviewed.
privacy: Reading Logia needs no account, and Logia sets no cookies of its own. If you sign in to save or like comments, you use your Open Word Bible account, and what you save is kept there.
about.privacy_counter: To learn which books and pages people read, Logia counts visits with GoatCounter. It sets no cookies, keeps no IP addresses and builds no profile of anyone; it records only the page, the site you came from, and your browser, screen size and country in general terms.
open: Copy, change and publish it, with no permission needed and no credit required.
Build on the site's code, keeping its licence notice.
The Open Word Bible, free in the same way.
about.open_note: The Greek and Hebrew word data and the cross-references carry their own licences, listed on the open data page.
about.cite: To cite Logia as a whole:
about.citation: Logia: a free library of Christian commentary. {url}
about.cite_note: To quote one excerpt, use the Cite button beside it, which names the edition it was copied from.
about.help: A script checks every excerpt, but people catch what scripts miss.
help_items: Seen a word the scanner got wrong? Tell us the verse and the word.
Published in 1930 or earlier, with a scan or transcription online.
When Logia adds a language, each translation is approved by a native speaker.
about.thanks: Logia stands on the work of others.
thanks_sefaria: The example of an open library of commentary, for Jewish texts.
questions: Why only books published in 1930 or earlier?

So that every text is in the public domain in the United States and free for anyone to copy. Most later commentaries are still under copyright. Each work's page records its edition and what is still to be confirmed for other countries.
No. Spelling, punctuation and the translator's English are kept as printed. Only plain misreadings by a scanner are fixed, and every fix is listed.
Is any of it written by AI?

No commentary is. Every excerpt is copied from its edition and checked against it by a script. Where Logia adds writing of its own, such as a guide or a biography, it is marked as a draft until a person reviews it.
Why isn't my favourite commentator here?
Logia adds one commentary at a time, and only from an edition published in 1930 or earlier with a readable scan or transcription. You can suggest one above.
Yes. The commentaries are in the public domain and Logia's data is CC0, so you may copy them into a sermon, a class handout or an app without asking.

occasions.index_heading: Readings from John through the church year
occasions.index_dek: Many churches read from John on the great days of the year. Each page sets the reading beside everything Logia holds on it, from the early church to the 1800s.

occasions.index_description: The Gospel readings from John for Christmas, Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, each with what the church fathers and later commentators wrote on it.

christmas.name: Christmas Day
christmas.intro: John's prologue is read on Christmas Day. The Revised Common Lectionary and the Book of Common Prayer read John 1:1–14, and the Roman Missal reads John 1:1–18 at the Mass during the Day. Below is what the church has said about it, from the early church to the 1800s.
christmas.read: Revised Common Lectionary and Book of Common Prayer: John 1:1–14. Roman Missal: John 1:1–18.

maundy-thursday.name: Maundy Thursday
maundy-thursday.intro: On Maundy Thursday many churches read John's account of Jesus washing his disciples' feet. The Revised Common Lectionary reads John 13:1–17 and 31b–35, and the Roman Missal reads John 13:1–15 at the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper. This page shows John 13:1–17.
maundy-thursday.read: Revised Common Lectionary: John 13:1–17, 31b–35. Roman Missal: John 13:1–15.

good-friday.name: Good Friday
good-friday.intro: On Good Friday the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman Missal both read the Passion according to John, John 18:1–19:42.
good-friday.read: Revised Common Lectionary and Roman Missal: John 18:1–19:42.

easter.name: Easter Day
easter.intro: On Easter Day many churches read John's account of the empty tomb. The Revised Common Lectionary gives John 20:1–18, and the Roman Missal reads John 20:1–9 at the Mass of the day. This page shows John 20:1–18.
easter.read: Revised Common Lectionary: John 20:1–18. Roman Missal: John 20:1–9.

second-sunday-of-easter.name: Second Sunday of Easter
second-sunday-of-easter.heading: The Gospel for the Second Sunday of Easter: {ref}
second-sunday-of-easter.intro: On the Sunday after Easter the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman Missal read John 20:19–31 every year: Jesus appears to the disciples, and then to Thomas. The Orthodox Church reads it on Thomas Sunday.
second-sunday-of-easter.read: Revised Common Lectionary and Roman Missal, every year: John 20:19–31. Orthodox: Thomas Sunday.

pentecost.name: Pentecost
pentecost.intro: At Pentecost in Year B, the year that begins in Advent 2026, the Revised Common Lectionary reads Jesus's promise of the Advocate, John 15:26–27 and 16:4b–15. This page shows the whole of John 15:26–16:15.
pentecost.read: Revised Common Lectionary, Year B: John 15:26–27; 16:4b–15.

i-am.heading: The seven “I am” sayings in John
i-am.title: The “I am” sayings of Jesus in John: what the church fathers and later commentators said
i-am.description: The seven “I am” sayings in the Gospel of John, from the bread of life to the true vine, with what Chrysostom, Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin and others wrote on each.
i-am.dek: Seven times in John, Jesus says “I am” with an image: bread, light, a door, a shepherd, the resurrection, the way, a vine. Here is each saying in the Open Word Bible, with what the commentators in Logia wrote on it.
i-am.note: John also records “I am” with no image after it, as in 8:58, “before Abraham was, I am.”

items.way: The way, the truth, and the life

signs.heading: The seven signs in John
signs.title: The seven signs in the Gospel of John: what the church fathers and later commentators said
signs.description: The seven signs in John, from water made wine at Cana to the raising of Lazarus, with what Chrysostom, Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin and others wrote on each.
signs.dek: John calls Jesus's miracles signs. He numbers the first two, at Cana (2:11) and the healing of the official's son (4:54), and ends by saying Jesus did many other signs not written in his book (20:30). Here are the seven usually counted, each with what the commentators in Logia wrote on it.
signs.note: Lists of the seven differ. Some count the catch of fish in John 21 in place of the walking on the sea, and some count the resurrection itself as the last sign.

plan.dek: Read the whole of {book} through Lent {year}, from Ash Wednesday, {start}, to Holy Saturday, the day before Easter on {easter}. Each day's passages open with everything Logia holds on them, from the early church to the 1800s.
plan.note: Sundays are not counted in Lent's forty days, so the plan leaves them free. Each day has about the same number of verses, kept to whole passages.
plan.easter_link: On Easter Day, read the Gospel for Easter.

cited.heading: The Scripture the commentators cite on {book}
cited.description: Which books and verses of the Bible did the church fathers and later commentators cite most when explaining {book}? {n} citations, counted from Logia's public-domain library.
cited.dek: Explaining {book}, the commentators in Logia cite Scripture {n} times: {own} times another verse of {book} itself, and {ot} times the Old Testament, across {others} other books in all.
cited.outside_title: The {n} passages cited most from the rest of Scripture
cited.inside_title: The {n} verses of {book} cited most within it
cited.inside_note: A commentator explaining one verse of {book} often cites another verse of the same book.
cited.how: Each citation is a reference to Scripture printed in an excerpt, such as “(1 Timothy 3:16)”, found by a script that reads the excerpts. None has yet been checked by a person, so a few may be misreadings. A passage is counted each time any excerpt cites it. How often a commentary cites Scripture depends on its style and on how much of it Logia holds.

catena.heading: Who Aquinas quotes in the Catena Aurea on John
catena.description: Thomas Aquinas built his Catena Aurea on John from the Fathers: Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Alcuin, Origen, Bede and others. {n} quotations, counted from the edition in Logia.
catena.dek: Thomas Aquinas wrote the Catena Aurea as a chain of quotations from the Fathers, each opened by its author's name. In Logia's excerpts on John, {n} quotations name {k} sources.
catena.held: Logia holds {name}'s own work on John, and links each quotation it can trace to the passage it comes from.
catena.how: Each quotation is counted by the name printed at its head in {edition}: “CHRYS.” for Chrysostom, “AUG.” for Augustine. A name the scan misread is not counted, so the true numbers are a little higher.

guide.draft_note: Logia wrote this page; it is not commentary. It is a draft until a named reviewer approves it.

llms.holds: It holds {excerpts} excerpts from {works} commentaries by {authors} commentators, on {books}, each tied to the verses it comments on.
llms.rules: Every excerpt is copied word for word from a public-domain edition (published in 1930 or earlier) and links to its source; nothing is paraphrased or summarised. Logia takes no side where Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings differ. The Bible text is the Open Word Bible (CC0), an AI draft awaiting human review. Logia's data is CC0.
address_list: one verse with everything on it: each commentator's excerpts in full, who cites the verse elsewhere, the whole homilies on it, the Greek words, translation notes and cross-references. Every verse with commentary has one (book code, chapter, verse).
the chapter reader: the Bible text, with the commentary on each verse in a panel.
a book: its chapters and who comments on it.
a commentator: dates, tradition, a short biography and every comment.
a commentary: its edition, translator, rights and source, and every excerpt in order.
every excerpt as JSON, with its verses, work and source (also logia-en.csv).

llms.cite_how: Name the commentator, the work and the edition, then the Logia address of the verse, for example: John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of St. John, Homily 27 (Oxford translation), quoted at https://logia.faith/jhn/3/16/.
